summary: Following the Prophet's ﷺ death, several tribes across Arabia renounced Islam or withheld zakat, and multiple false prophets arose. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq ؓ, as Caliph, resolved to fight all apostasy and refuse any compromise on the obligations of Islam. The military campaigns — led primarily by Khalid ibn al-Walid ؓ — restored unity across Arabia within a year.
narrative:
The death of the Prophet ﷺ triggered an immediate crisis of political and religious unity across Arabia. The Bay'ah given to the Prophet ﷺ was, in the understanding of many tribal leaders, a personal covenant — not a permanent submission to the Islamic state. Three categories of defection appeared almost simultaneously: first, outright apostasy by tribes that renounced Islam entirely; second, tribes that accepted Islam but refused to pay zakat, arguing the obligation had been personal to the Prophet ﷺ; and third, the emergence of false prophets who claimed prophethood for themselves.

Among the most significant false prophets were Musaylimah ibn Habib al-Hanafi of the Banu Hanifah in Yamama — who had sent the Prophet ﷺ a letter claiming equal prophethood during the Year of Delegations and received the famous reply — and al-Aswad al-Ansi of Yemen, who had actually seized control of much of Yemen before being killed on the very night of the Prophet's ﷺ death by insiders. Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid of the Banu Asad also claimed prophethood and drew significant followers before his defeat and eventual return to Islam.

Abu Bakr's position was firm from the beginning. Al-Tabari records that some companions, including Umar ibn al-Khattab ؓ, initially counselled leniency toward those who withheld only zakat but accepted the rest of Islam. Abu Bakr ؓ rejected this and his position became one of the defining declarations of early Islamic governance: 'By Allah, I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakat. Zakat is the right that falls on wealth. By Allah, if they withhold from me even a hobbling rope that they used to give to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, I will fight them for withholding it.' Umar ؓ later said that he realised Allah had opened Abu Bakr's chest for the fight and that he came to know that Abu Bakr was right.

Khalid ibn al-Walid ؓ, the supreme military commander of the Ridda campaigns, was dispatched in several directions. He first defeated Tulayha and the Banu Asad, then moved against other apostate groups in the north and centre of Arabia. His most consequential campaign was against Musaylimah at the Battle of Yamama in 11 or early 12 AH — the bloodiest battle of the entire Ridda period.

At Yamama, the Banu Hanifah — among the finest warriors in Arabia — fought with ferocious discipline behind Musaylimah. The Muslims took heavy casualties in the initial engagement. The battle's turning point came in a walled garden — al-Hadiqah — where the surviving Banu Hanifah fighters had retreated. The garden became known as 'Hadiqat al-Mawt' — the Garden of Death — for the carnage within it. Wahshi ibn Harb ؓ — who had killed Hamzah ؓ at Uhud and had accepted Islam — threw his javelin and killed Musaylimah. Abu Dujana ؓ may also have struck the fatal blow; the sources record both. With Musaylimah's death, the Banu Hanifah surrendered.

The losses among the Muslim force at Yamama were severe, and crucially, they included a large number of companions who had memorised the Quran (the qurra). It was this loss that prompted Umar ibn al-Khattab ؓ to approach Abu Bakr ؓ with urgency about the need to compile the Quran — an account that forms the opening of the compilation narrative. Ibn Kathir records that approximately 70 of those who had memorised the Quran were killed at Yamama.

Within approximately a year after the Prophet's ﷺ death, all of Arabia had been brought back under the authority of the Islamic state. The Ridda Wars demonstrated the principled inflexibility of Abu Bakr ؓ on the core obligations of Islam, established the precedent that the state had authority to enforce its pillars, and set in motion the rapid military expansion into Persia and Byzantium that would follow under both Abu Bakr ؓ and Umar ؓ.
